f: What core functions does an investment bank perform for a company raising capital?
b:
• Advises on the best way to raise long-term capital
  • Distributes the new securities to raise the money
  • Buys the issue from the company and resells it to investors (underwriting)
  • Places large blocks with the public and institutions
  • Helps the issuer comply with securities law

f: Distinguish a firm commitment underwriting from a best efforts underwriting.
b:
Firm commitment — the underwriter buys the whole issue and guarantees the company its money; unsold shares are the underwriter's loss.
Best efforts — no guarantee; the underwriter sells what it can and the company gets nothing for shares left unsold.
Tell: who eats an unsold issue?

f: Distinguish a broker from a dealer, and say what a dealer is called on an exchange vs. over the counter.
b:
Broker — an agent for the customer, paid a commission.
Dealer — a principal trading for its own account; it buys at its bid and sells at its ask.
Dealer = specialist on an exchange, market maker over the counter. Firms doing both are broker-dealers.

f: What are the defining investment traits of venture capital?
b:
Financing for privately held (often start-up) companies, typically through convertible preferred stock.
  • High risk, high potential return — some deals are total losses
  • Illiquid; low correlation with stocks
  • VC firm takes a large equity stake and helps manage
  • Goal: cash out in about 5–10 years, ideally via an IPO

f: Under Reg D Rule 501, how does an individual qualify as an accredited investor?
b:
Meet either test (2026 edition figure):
  • Net worth over $1 million, alone or with a spouse, excluding the primary residence, or
  • Income over $200,000 alone (or $300,000 joint) in each of the two most recent years, with a reasonable expectation of the same this year
Directors, executive officers and general partners of the issuer also qualify.

f: Distinguish the general partner from the limited partners in a limited partnership.
b:
General partner — runs the business, decides when distributions are paid, carries unlimited liability.
Limited partners — no role in management, limited liability; they share in income, gains, losses, deductions and credits.
Drawbacks for LPs: riskier than bonds or listed stock, usually illiquid, resale may be restricted.

f: Distinguish the primary market from the secondary market.
b:
Primary — first sale of newly issued securities; investors' money (less underwriting costs) flows to the issuing company.
Secondary — investors trade already-issued securities with one another; the issuer receives nothing.

f: Once the stop price is hit, how does a stop order differ from a stop-limit order?
b:
Both are triggered when the stock trades at or through the stop price.
Stop → becomes a market order: you get out, but a gap can fill you well below the stop.
Stop-limit → becomes a limit order: price is protected, but the trade may never execute if the stock keeps falling.

f: Where is a sell stop placed versus a buy stop, and who uses each?
b:
Sell stop — set below the current price; a long holder uses it to cut losses or protect gains in a falling market.
Buy stop — set above the current price; a short seller uses it to cap losses by buying to cover in a rising market.

f: What formula gives the stock price that triggers a margin call?
b:
Margin-call price = [purchase price × (1 − initial margin %)] ÷ (1 − maintenance margin %)
The numerator is the loan per share (debit balance per share), so it is also loan per share ÷ (1 − maintenance %).
At or below that price, equity is under the maintenance requirement and the broker demands cash.

f: Distinguish initial margin from maintenance margin.
b:
Initial margin — the share of the purchase the investor must put up: 50% under Federal Reserve Regulation T (2026 edition figure); a broker may demand more.
Maintenance margin — minimum equity % that must remain afterward; set by the broker (often 35%), with a 25% floor under NYSE Rule 431(b). Always lower than the initial margin.

f: How does the holding period return formula change when stock is bought on margin?
b:
Normal: HPR = (ending value − beginning value ± cash flows) ÷ beginning value.
On margin: same numerator, with margin interest as a negative cash flow, but divide by the investor's own initial investment (the equity put up).
Leverage magnifies the percentage gain — and the percentage loss.

f: A client is short a stock when it pays a dividend. What does the client owe, and how does it affect the return?
b:
The short seller must pay the lender of the shares a cash amount equal to the dividend.
Net profit = sale proceeds − cost to buy back − dividends paid
% return = net profit ÷ margin deposit (proceeds × initial margin %).

f: Distinguish liquidity from marketability, and name an asset that is liquid but not marketable.
b:
Liquidity — convertible to cash quickly at a known price without a meaningful loss of principal.
Marketability — can be sold quickly in an identifiable market, with no promise about price.
A money market deposit account is liquid but not marketable (only the bank redeems it); a T-bill is both.

f: Which suits a client who wants federal deposit insurance on her cash reserve: a money market deposit account (MMDA) or a money market mutual fund?
b:
The MMDA. It is a bank deposit, FDIC-insured to $250,000 per ownership category (2026 edition figure), with a minimum balance and limited checks/transfers.
A money market mutual fund is run by an open-end investment company, holds T-bills, commercial paper and negotiable CDs, and is not federally insured.

f: How is the return on a U.S. Treasury bill taxed?
b:
The bill is bought at a discount; the discount is the interest.
  • Federal: ordinary income, taxed when the bill matures
  • State and local: exempt
  • Not subject to OID rules (maturity of one year or less)
  • Sold before maturity: the gap between sale price and purchase price is taxable

f: What are the key features of commercial paper?
b:
Unsecured, negotiable short-term note issued by a large corporation to fund receivables and inventory.
  • Usually $100,000+ denominations; sold at a discount
  • Maturity of 270 days or less; rated for quality; often backed by bank credit lines
  • A bit less liquid and riskier than T-bills → slightly higher yield
  • Interest = ordinary income; money market funds are the main buyers

f: Distinguish a repurchase agreement (repo) from a reverse repo.
b:
Repo — a dealer sells government securities and agrees to buy them back later at a set, higher price. Legally a sale, in substance a collateralized loan to the dealer; the price gap is the interest (repo rate).
Reverse repo — the dealer buys the securities and later sells them back at a higher price, so the dealer is the lender.

f: A retiree says keeping most of her portfolio in CDs and money market accounts is the safe choice. What's wrong with that assumption?
b: It trades default risk for purchasing power risk: inflation steadily erodes what the interest and principal can buy. The textbook flags loss of purchasing power, not loss of principal, as one of the biggest threats to a retiree's income.

f: What is the order of the capital gain and loss netting process?
b:
1. Net short-term gains against short-term losses.
2. Net long-term gains against long-term losses.
3. If one side is a gain and the other a loss, net them to a single figure.
4. Net ST gain → ordinary rates; net LT gain → 0%/15%/20% (2026 edition figure). Net loss → deduct up to $3,000 a year and carry the rest forward indefinitely.

f: After netting, Rhea has a $7,500 net capital loss and no other capital transactions. How much can she deduct this year, and what happens to the rest?
b: She deducts $3,000 this year (2026 edition figure) and carries the remaining $4,500 forward; unused capital losses carry forward indefinitely.

f: What triggers the wash sale rule, and what happens to the disallowed loss?
b:
A sale of stock or securities at a loss when similar securities are acquired within 30 days before or after the sale (2026 edition figure).
The loss is not recognized now; it is added to the basis of the replacement shares:
New basis = cost of replacement shares + disallowed loss.

f: What holding period must a stock meet for its dividend to get the preferential qualified-dividend rates?
b: It must be held more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date (2026 edition figure). Fall short and the preferential 0%/15%/20% rates don't apply.

f: Why don't REIT and S corporation dividends get the preferential qualified-dividend rates?
b: Qualified dividends come from C corporations, whose income is taxed at the corporate level before it is paid out. REITs and S corporations are not taxed at the entity level before distributing, so their dividends don't get the preferential capital-gain rates.

f: How is the net investment income tax (NIIT) calculated?
b:
NIIT = 3.8% × the lesser of:
  • net investment income, or
  • MAGI above the threshold — $250,000 MFJ, $125,000 MFS, $200,000 all others
(2026 edition figure; textbook example thresholds.) Net investment income is investment income less certain deductible investment expenses, such as investment interest expense and early-withdrawal penalties on savings.

f: How is interest from Treasuries, corporate bonds and municipal bonds taxed at the federal and state level?
b:
Treasuries — federal yes, state no.
Corporate bonds — federal yes, state yes.
Municipal bonds — federal no (limited exceptions); state yes unless issued in the investor's home state, which can make in-state munis double tax-exempt.

f: Distinguish a secured bond from a debenture.
b:
Secured bond — pledges specific assets that bondholders can sell if the issuer misses interest or principal.
Debenture — unsecured; backed only by the issuer's credit and reputation, so it yields more than a secured bond of the same issuer and term.
A subordinated debenture ranks behind other creditors and pays more still, yet sits ahead of common stock.

f: What three drawbacks does a call feature create for the bondholder?
b:
• Cash flows are uncertain (the bond may disappear early).
  • Calls happen after rates drop, so proceeds are reinvested at lower rates (reinvestment risk).
  • Price gains are capped: the bond rarely trades far above its call price once a call is expected.
Issuers call to refinance at a lower coupon; corporate indentures generally give at least 10 years of call protection.

f: Where is the dividing line between investment-grade and high-yield (junk) bonds?
b:
Investment grade = the top four categories: BBB− or better (S&P) or Baa or better (Moody's).
Below that (BB+ / Ba and lower) is noninvestment grade, with higher default risk and higher yields. Some institutions may buy only investment-grade issues.

f: Distinguish interest rate risk from reinvestment rate risk.
b:
Interest rate risk — rates rise → the fixed cash flows are discounted at a higher rate → price falls.
Reinvestment rate risk — rates fall → coupons (and returned principal) are reinvested at lower rates, so the realized return can fall short of the promised YTM.
They pull in opposite directions; for exam purposes a zero-coupon bond has no reinvestment rate risk.

f: What are Treasury STRIPS, and why are they best held in a tax-deferred account?
b:
Zero-coupon bonds made by separating each coupon and the principal of a T-note or T-bond into its own security. Bought through brokers, dealers and institutions (not from the Treasury), at a deep discount; very rate-sensitive, no call risk, virtually no default or liquidity risk.
Tax: interest is taxed as ordinary income as it accrues even though no cash is paid (phantom income) → tax-deferred account.

f: How do TIPS protect against inflation, and how is the inflation adjustment taxed?
b:
Principal is indexed to the CPI. Each six months the payment = adjusted principal × (fixed coupon rate ÷ 2), so the rate stays fixed but the dollar coupon moves. At maturity the holder gets the greater of original or adjusted principal.
Tax: interest and any upward principal adjustment are federal ordinary income in the year they occur (adjustment raises basis); no state or local income tax.

f: Which agency securities have the direct backing of the U.S. government, and which only indirect backing?
b:
Direct: GNMA (Ginnie Mae) and the Farm Credit Administration.
Indirect: FHLMC (Freddie Mac), FNMA (Fannie Mae), SLMA (Sallie Mae) — so they pay slightly higher coupons.
Unlike Treasuries, agency interest is generally taxable at federal, state and local levels. (Fannie and Freddie have been in FHFA conservatorship since 2008.)

f: Distinguish prepayment risk from extension risk in mortgage pass-throughs.
b:
Prepayment risk — rates fall → homeowners refinance → principal returns early and must be reinvested at lower rates; price gains are limited (an embedded call).
Extension risk — rates rise → prepayments slow → average life lengthens and expected principal arrives later, lowering the return.

f: Distinguish general obligation (GO) bonds from revenue bonds.
b:
GO bonds — fund projects that earn no revenue; repaid from the municipality's taxes (full faith and credit); usually need voter approval; debt limits protect holders → lower risk.
Revenue bonds — repaid only from the income of the financed facility (e.g., an airport) → riskier, so higher yields for similar maturities.

f: What is the taxable equivalent yield (TEY) formula, and when do you use it?
b:
TEY = tax-exempt yield ÷ (1 − marginal tax rate)
Use it to restate a muni yield as the taxable yield a corporate bond must beat. The mirror formula is after-tax yield = taxable yield × (1 − marginal rate).
The higher the bracket, the bigger the edge for tax-exempt income.

f: Distinguish original issue discount (OID) from market discount for tax purposes.
b:
OID — issued below par. A computed slice of the discount is income every year (phantom income), and basis rises by that amount.
Market discount — issued at par but bought later below par because its value fell. Generally not taxed until sale or maturity, then treated as interest income; only gain beyond the accrued market discount is capital gain. (An election to accrue it yearly exists but is rarely used.)

f: Which client need do zero-coupon bonds fit best, and what is their main tax drawback?
b:
Fit: a known sum on a known date (e.g., tuition) — no reinvestment rate risk, and the deep discount buys more face value per dollar.
Drawback: taxable zeros create phantom income — accrued interest is taxed yearly though no cash arrives → hold in a retirement or other tax-deferred account. Prices are also more volatile than coupon bonds of similar quality.

f: Distinguish Yankee bonds, Eurodollar bonds, and Eurobonds.
b:
Yankee — foreign issuer, U.S.-dollar denominated, sold and traded in the U.S. → no currency risk for a U.S. investor.
Eurodollar — U.S.-dollar bonds sold outside the U.S. by non-U.S. issuers through a non-U.S. syndicate; no SEC registration.
Eurobond — denominated in a currency not native to the country where issued (any currency, not just euros); sold by international syndicates.

f: What is the conversion ratio formula?
b:
Conversion ratio = par value ÷ conversion price
= the number of shares each bond converts into. The conversion price is the stock price at which the exchange happens.
E.g., $1,000 par ÷ $20 conversion price = 50 shares.

f: How do you calculate a convertible bond's conversion value?
b:
Conversion value = conversion ratio × current market price of the stock
It is what the bond would be worth if converted today. E.g., 50 shares × $23 = $1,150.

f: What is a convertible bond's investment value, and how is it found?
b:
Its value as a straight (nonconvertible) bond — the PV of the semiannual coupons plus par, discounted at the market rate for comparable straight bonds.
It is the cushion under the price if the stock collapses, and it moves whenever interest rates move.

f: What is the lowest price a convertible bond should trade for?
b: The greater of its investment (straight) value or its conversion value. If it traded below conversion value, buyers would snap it up and convert; below straight value, it would be cheap as a bond.

f: Distinguish the conversion premium from the investment premium.
b:
Conversion premium = market price − conversion value; % = ÷ conversion value. (Premium over the bond's worth as stock.)
Investment premium = market price − investment value; % = ÷ investment value. (Premium paid for the conversion option over its worth as a bond.)

f: How is a convertible's downside risk measured, and what is the classic percentage mistake?
b:
Dollar downside risk = market price − investment value (the same dollars as the investment premium).
Percentage downside risk = that difference ÷ market price — not ÷ investment value. It measures how far the price could fall from today's price to the straight-bond floor. It changes as rates change.

f: What is portfolio immunization, and when is the offset complete?
b:
A technique that sets price (interest rate) risk against reinvestment rate risk: if rates rise, prices fall but coupons reinvest higher, and vice versa.
Full offset when portfolio duration = duration of the liability (the investor's time horizon).
Not passive: portfolio duration drifts down faster than the liability's, so periodic rebalancing is needed.

f: How can a family immunize a known college bill with a single bond?
b:
Buy a zero-coupon bond maturing when the money is needed — a zero's duration equals its maturity, so duration matches the horizon exactly.
A coupon bond's duration is shorter than its maturity, so a coupon bond would need to mature somewhat after the target date.

f: What is a bond ladder, and what are its two advantages?
b:
Equal slices spread across staggered maturities (e.g., 1 through 5 years); each maturing rung is rolled to the long end.
  • Higher yield than an all-short-term portfolio.
  • Regular maturities supply cash to reinvest, keep the structure intact and limit damage from rising rates.
A long-term, relatively passive strategy.

f: How is a barbell structured, and why does it need active management?
b:
Only short-term and long-term bonds — nothing in the middle (also called a dumbbell). The long end locks in long rates; the short end keeps money free to use elsewhere if bonds fall.
Short bonds keep maturing, so proceeds must be redeployed to hold the shape → active management.

f: How does a bullet strategy work, and what is it designed to do?
b:
Bonds are bought at different times so that they all mature on one target date (e.g., an 8-year bond now, a 6-year in two years, a 4-year in four years).
Purpose: match duration to a single future cash need and minimize interest rate risk.

f: Distinguish a substitution swap from an intermarket spread swap.
b:
Substitution — swap into a bond with identical characteristics that is priced differently; a short-lived arbitrage until the market corrects.
Intermarket spread — swap between bond sectors (e.g., governments ↔ corporates) because one sector looks mispriced relative to the other; aims to exploit a YTM gap across markets.

f: A manager expects interest rates to rise. Which swap fits, and what does she do?
b: A rate anticipation swap: sell long-term bonds and buy short-term bonds to cut price sensitivity. If she expected rates to fall, she would do the reverse (short → long).

f: Which bond traits raise relative price swings, and how should a portfolio be built for a rate forecast?
b:
Bigger price swings come with a lower coupon, longer maturity and lower YTM.
Expect falling rates → long maturities, low coupons (maximum sensitivity, capture gains).
Expect rising rates → short maturities, high coupons (minimum sensitivity, limit losses).

f: Why should a newly retired couple not keep all of their bond money in T-bills?
b: Time horizon matters more than age. A 60- or 65-year-old may live 20+ more years, and a couple's joint horizon can be longer. With a horizon beyond about 10 years, the portfolio needs more than T-bills.

f: Why does the textbook suggest a TIPS ladder inside a traditional IRA for retirees?
b:
Staggered TIPS maturities deliver inflation-adjusted cash each year. Held to maturity they carry no default, call or interest rate risk and little purchasing power risk.
Inside a traditional IRA, the yearly inflation step-ups on unmatured bonds are not taxed currently (avoiding phantom income).

f: What does each yield curve shape typically signal?
b:
• Normal (upward) — economic expansion; rates expected to rise.
  • Flat — economy near a peak; little change in rates expected.
  • Inverted — Fed has tightened in an inflationary economy; rates expected to fall; may signal recession.
  • Humped — middle maturities yield the most.

f: Name the three yield curve theories, and say which one explains only an upward-sloping curve.
b:
Unbiased expectations, liquidity preference, and market segmentation.
Liquidity preference explains only a normal (upward) curve; the other two can explain any shape.

f: What does the unbiased expectations theory say, and what is its formula?
b:
Long-term rates are the geometric mean of today's short rate and expected future short rates.
1 + RN = [(1 + R1)(1 + E(r2)) … (1 + E(rN))]1/N
Expected higher short rates → upward curve; expected lower short rates → inverted curve.

f: What does the liquidity preference theory assume about investors?
b: Investors prefer short-term bonds (less price volatility, easier to turn into predictable cash), so they must be paid a liquidity premium to lend long. Result: the curve should slope upward; other shapes are temporary aberrations.

f: What drives the shape of the yield curve under market segmentation theory?
b: Supply and demand inside separate maturity segments. Institutions match assets to liabilities (banks lend short, savings and loans intermediate, life insurers long) and stay in their segment; in the strong form they never cross segments for extra yield. So the curve reflects institutional maturity needs and can take any shape.

f: With an inverted yield curve, why does the textbook favor long-term bonds over higher-yielding short-term paper?
b: When the curve returns to normal, all rates fall but short rates fall the most. Long bonds lock in the high rate and gain the most price; short paper simply matures and is reinvested at lower rates. Income buyers should insist on call protection.

f: Why is preferred stock called a hybrid security?
b:
Bond-like: fixed dividend set as a % of par; no vote; no share of profits; paid ahead of common; price moves inversely with rates.
Equity-like: the board must declare the dividend (not guaranteed); a missed dividend does not trigger bankruptcy; no maturity date (a perpetuity), so holders must sell to get their money back.

f: What does a cumulative feature give preferred shareholders?
b: Any skipped preferred dividends from prior years (arrears) must be paid, along with the current preferred dividend, before common shareholders receive any dividend.

f: How do you value a no-growth preferred stock, and why is it more rate-sensitive than the issuer's bonds?
b:
V = D ÷ r (a perpetuity: annual dividend ÷ required return or market yield on similar preferreds).
With no maturity date, its price swings more than the same company's bonds for a given rate change → buy in steady or falling rate environments.

f: What dividends-received deduction can a corporation take on preferred dividends it receives?
b: Subject to limits: 50% of dividends received if it owns less than 20% of the payer; 65% if it owns 20% or more (2026 edition figure). It applies to dividends from domestic corporations, not to bond interest.

f: Distinguish a common stockholder's claim on a corporation from a bondholder's claim.
b:
Stockholder = owner: a proportionate share of assets and earnings, voting rights, dividends only if declared, no fixed payment.
Bondholder = creditor: fixed payments plus return of principal, no ownership, but ranks ahead of stockholders in default or liquidation.

f: Name the seven types of common stock this module describes.
b:
• Blue-chip
  • Growth (incl. emerging growth)
  • Income
  • Value
  • Cyclical
  • Defensive
  • Technology

f: Distinguish cyclical stocks from defensive stocks.
b:
Cyclical: profits swing with the economy — strong in expansions, weak in downturns (automakers, consumer discretionary, restaurants).
Defensive: little affected by the business cycle; slow, steady growth; sell everyday necessities (grocery chains); favored in recessions, lag in booms.

f: Distinguish growth stocks from value stocks.
b:
Growth: sales and earnings growing faster than the industry average; usually little or no dividend because earnings are reinvested.
Value: price looks cheap versus the firm's historical earnings and asset values; the bet is that the market will eventually reprice it.
Over time a growth stock can turn into a value stock.

f: Name the four equity risks this module lists, with a one-line meaning for each.
b:
• Market — most stocks move with the overall market.
  • Interest rate — rising rates push stock values down; falling rates help.
  • Business — risk tied to the specific firm (its speculative nature, management, philosophy).
  • Financial — added risk when the firm finances assets with debt (leverage).

f: Distinguish subscription rights from warrants.
b:
Rights: short life (a few weeks); exercise price below market at issue; given to existing holders (usually one per share) so they can keep their ownership percentage.
Warrants: long life (often up to 5+ years); exercise price above market at issue; attached as a sweetener to a bond or preferred issue.
Both can trade separately.

f: How does a warrant differ from an exchange-listed call option?
b:
• Issued by the corporation; a call is written by an individual.
  • Customized terms; a call has standardized OCC terms.
  • Maturity of several years; a call normally expires within nine months.
  • Usually not tied to a 100-share round lot.

f: What is the ex-dividend date, and when must an investor buy to receive a declared dividend?
b: The ex-dividend date is the first trading day on which a buyer is not entitled to the already-declared dividend. To be a shareholder of record (and get the dividend), the investor must buy before the ex-dividend date. The book ties this to T+1 settlement (adopted May 2024) (2026 edition figure).

f: What is the dividend payout ratio, and how is it calculated?
b:
The share of earnings paid out as dividends.
Payout ratio = dividends per share ÷ earnings per share
Example: $1.50 dividend ÷ $5.00 EPS = 30%.

f: What two tests make a common-stock dividend 'qualified' for long-term capital gain rates?
b:
1. Paid by a domestic or qualified foreign corporation (incl. ADRs readily tradable on a U.S. market).
2. Stock held more than 60 days in the 121-day window that starts 60 days before the ex-dividend date (2026 edition figure).
Qualified rates: 0%, 15%, 20% (2026 edition figure). Nonqualified dividends: ordinary rates.

f: How are dividends reinvested through a DRIP taxed, and how do they affect basis?
b: Taxed exactly like cash dividends in the year paid. Unlike a cash dividend, the reinvested amount is added to basis, so it is not taxed again when the shares are sold.

f: After a stock dividend, what happens to the company's total value, the share price and the holder's basis per share?
b:
• Total market value: theoretically unchanged (a recapitalization; assets and liabilities unchanged).
  • Price per share: falls in proportion (dilution).
  • Tax: generally none, unless the holder could have elected cash (constructive receipt).
  • Basis: same total, spread over more shares → lower basis per share.

f: Distinguish a stock split from a reverse stock split.
b:
Split (e.g., 2-for-1): par value cut, shares up, price down — makes shares cheaper for small investors.
Reverse split (e.g., 1-for-4): shares down, price up — helps avoid delisting and looks more attractive.
Neither changes the holder's ownership percentage or total value; not taxable; basis per share is adjusted.

f: How is a mutual fund's NAV per share calculated, and at what price is an order filled?
b:
NAV per share = (total assets − liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding; assets include cash, not just securities.
Computed at least once each business day, usually after the 4:00 p.m. ET NYSE close. Orders get the next NAV computed after the order (forward pricing).

f: Distinguish Class A, Class B and Class C mutual fund shares.
b:
A: front-end load added at purchase; generally lowest total cost → suits long horizons.
B: back-end load (CDSC) if sold within a set period; may be waived after about five years.
C: level load — an asset-based annual 12b-1 fee acts as the sales charge.

f: What three categories make up a fund's total annual operating expenses?
b:
• Management fee — pays the advisor (portfolio managers, analysts, research).
  • 12b-1 fee — first for marketing; now mostly ongoing pay for selling the fund (a 'hidden load' even in some no-load funds).
  • Other expenses — recordkeeping, audit, custody, legal, proxies, directors' fees, state/local taxes.
Paid from fund income.

f: Name four ways a bond fund differs from an individual bond.
b:
1. Income changes over time as the portfolio is managed.
  2. No fixed maturity — no date when principal comes back.
  3. Income quoted as the SEC 30-day yield, not YTM or yield to call.
  4. Usually pays monthly, not semiannually.

f: Distinguish a single-state municipal bond fund from a national municipal bond fund.
b:
Single-state: in-state residents get interest free of federal and state tax (double exempt; sometimes local too = triple). Out-of-state residents usually skip it.
National: geographic diversification, but most interest is state-taxable; only the share from the holder's own state is state-exempt.
For both, check AMT exposure.

f: Distinguish a global equity fund from an international equity fund.
b:
Global: U.S. and foreign stocks.
International: foreign stocks only.
Foreign/international funds diversify more but carry more risk than global funds. Correlation with U.S. stocks: developed markets highest, emerging lower, frontier lowest.

f: Name the three forms of annual income a mutual fund investor receives and how each is taxed.
b:
• Ordinary dividends — taxable as dividends.
  • Exempt-interest dividends (e.g., muni fund) — free of federal income tax.
  • Capital gain distributions — typically long-term gain, however long the shares were held.
Reinvested distributions are still taxable (constructive receipt).

f: Distinguish a closed-end fund from an open-end mutual fund.
b:
Closed-end: fixed share count after the IPO; trades on an exchange or OTC; price set by supply and demand → premium or discount to NAV; can be bought on margin or sold short; no redemption pressure, so it can hold less-liquid assets.
Open-end: unlimited new shares; bought from and redeemed with the fund at NAV (plus any load).

f: What are the defining traits of a unit investment trust (UIT)?
b:
• Portfolio picked once and held (usually bonds) — passive, lower management fees.
  • No board, officers or investment advisor.
  • Limited life: liquidates and distributes proceeds at maturity (bond UITs may end early if calls shrink principal).
  • Income and gains pass through and are taxed to unit holders each year.

f: What is the main tax advantage of a separately managed account over a mutual fund?
b: The investor directly owns 100% of the securities, so each position carries its own cost basis — easier tax management. The client can also exclude specific holdings. Minimums are often $50,000 or more. A fund holder owns only a share of a pool.

f: What advantages do ETFs have over traditional mutual funds?
b:
• Trade all day at market prices (mutual funds use once-a-day forward pricing).
  • Usually lower expenses and lower turnover → more tax-efficient.
  • In-kind redemptions deliver securities, not taxable cash.
  • Can be bought on margin and sold short.

f: How is a hedge fund typically structured, and how is its manager paid?
b: Usually an unregistered, privately offered limited partnership: the manager is the general partner and investors are limited partners, mostly accredited and sophisticated. The manager is paid on performance (not on assets like a mutual fund manager) and often owns a large stake. Few disclosure requirements.

f: What are the trade-offs of a hedge fund of funds (FOF)?
b:
Pros: diversification across about 10–30 hedge funds; often more liquidity; a good entry-level option; can give nonaccredited investors access.
Cons: a second layer of fees; cash drag from reserves held for withdrawals; returns more correlated with stocks than single hedge funds.

f: How does a guaranteed investment contract (GIC) compare with a bank CD?
b: Similar idea (rate guaranteed for a fixed term, e.g., 5 years), but a GIC is issued by an insurance company and is not FDIC-insured, so it carries slightly more risk. Proceeds go mainly to commercial mortgages and investment-grade bonds. Main buyers: employers for 401(k) and pension plans.

f: Distinguish a participating GIC from a nonparticipating GIC.
b:
Participating: variable rate that follows interest rate changes → choose if rates are expected to rise.
Nonparticipating: fixed rate → choose if rates are expected to fall.

f: What is dollar cost averaging, and how is the average cost per share computed?
b:
Investing a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals (e.g., payroll or bank draft).
Average cost per share = total dollars invested ÷ total shares bought
The fixed amount buys more shares when prices are low. It does not guarantee a profit.

f: Distinguish average cost per share from average price per share under dollar cost averaging.
b:
Average cost = total dollars ÷ total shares (what each share really cost you).
Average price = simple mean of the prices on the purchase dates.
With a fixed dollar amount and changing prices, average cost is lower than average price, because more shares were bought at the low prices.

f: When does dollar cost averaging work well, and when does it work poorly?
b:
Works best: falling or fluctuating markets; it also limits the risk of a badly timed lump sum.
Works poorly: a steadily rising market — a lump sum up front would buy more shares.
A falling price may reflect a real problem; don't assume it will recover.

f: How does value averaging set each period's investment?
b:
Set a target increase in account value per period (e.g., +$1,000 a month).
Investment = target value − current value of shares held
It buys more when prices fall and less when they rise, and it sells if the account is above target. It needs more monitoring and nerve in down markets.

f: What is share averaging, and which investor does it suit?
b: Buy the same number of shares each period, so dollars spent rise as the price rises and fall as it falls — the mirror image of DCA. Average cost equals the simple average of the prices. Suits investors who can raise purchase amounts, and a momentum-style investor (DCA suits value style).

f: Name the three basis methods for mutual fund shares sold and rank them for a rising market.
b:
• Specific identification — generally most favorable (highest basis, least tax); needs detailed records and identifying the shares sold.
  • Average cost — most commonly used: total cost ÷ total shares.
  • FIFO — IRS default if shares aren't identified; generally least favorable when prices have risen.

f: What goes into a mutual fund shareholder's cost basis?
b: The purchase price of the shares plus commissions paid to buy them plus reinvested dividends and distributions. Reinvested exempt-interest dividends from a muni fund also add to basis, even though they were never taxed.

f: What is the starting point in choosing a mutual fund for a client, and what must the fund match?
b: Define and rank the client's objectives (current income, capital appreciation, capital preservation). The fund's objective must fit those objectives and the client's risk tolerance. The risk of the whole portfolio matters more than the risk of any one fund.

f: What does a fund's expense ratio include, and what does it leave out?
b:
Includes: management fee + 12b-1 fee + other operating expenses, as a % of average fund assets.
Excludes: sales loads paid by the investor and the fund's own trading costs (commissions, spreads).
Range: under 0.20% (some index funds) to 2.00%+.

f: How is portfolio turnover measured, and why is high turnover usually a negative?
b:
Turnover = lesser of purchases or sales ÷ average monthly assets
High turnover brings commissions, bid-ask costs and market-impact costs (none in the expense ratio) and often larger realized gains. It may signal market timing or a growth/momentum style.

f: Why does consistency matter more than one big year? Give the break-even math for a loss.
b: Big losses need even bigger gains to recover: required gain = loss ÷ (1 − loss). A 50% drop needs +100%. A fund that is steady in both bull and bear markets often ends ahead of a volatile one with a higher best year.

f: Over what time frame should a fund's performance be judged?
b: At least one full bull and one bear market cycle, so 5- and 10-year records; one year is too short. Also check how long the current manager has run the fund, since the record may belong to someone else.

f: What's wrong with assuming a growth fund creates little tax as long as you don't sell it?
b: It ignores capital gain distributions, which can be large in a bull-market year and are taxed even if reinvested. Short-term gains are taxed at ordinary rates. Buying just before a big distribution means buying a tax bill.

f: How is a bond's intrinsic value calculated?
b:
Discount every future cash flow (each semiannual coupon plus par at maturity) at the market yield per period and add them up:
PV = CF1/(1+y)1 + … + CFt/(1+y)t
Calculator (2 P/YR): N = years × 2, I/YR = comparable yield, PMT = annual coupon ÷ 2, FV = par, solve PV.

f: Why does an outstanding bond's price drop when market interest rates rise?
b: Its coupon is locked in at issue. A new buyer wants the higher market yield, so the only thing that can adjust is the price: it falls below par until the bond's YTM matches the new rate. Falling rates work the other way and push the price above par.

f: Quick call: a 3% coupon bond when comparable bonds now yield 4.5% — premium, par, or discount?
b: Discount. Whenever the market rate is above the coupon rate, the price must sit below par so the buyer earns the higher yield. Market rate below coupon → premium; equal → par.

f: For a callable bond trading at a premium, how do current yield, YTM and YTC rank?
b: CY > YTM > YTC. YTM and YTC both build in the loss of the premium as price drifts back to par (or call price); a call forces that loss sooner, so YTC is lowest — the worst case for the holder.

f: For a bond trading at a discount, how do the yields rank — and what happens at par?
b:
Discount: CY < YTM < YTC (YTM and YTC add the climb back up to par; a call delivers it sooner).
At par with no call premium: CY = YTM = YTC.

f: What does duration measure, and why is it quoted in years?
b: The weighted-average time to collect a bond's interest and principal, measured in present-value dollars (Macaulay's original definition — hence years). It doubles as a gauge of interest-rate sensitivity: the higher the duration, the bigger the price swing for a given rate change.

f: How do coupon rate, market yield and maturity each move duration?
b:
• Higher coupon → lower duration
  • Higher market yield → lower duration
  • Longer maturity → higher duration
Inverse to coupon and yield; direct with maturity.

f: What is a zero-coupon bond's duration, and how does a coupon bond's duration compare with its maturity?
b: A zero's duration equals its maturity (one cash flow, at the end), so it is always longer than a coupon bond of the same maturity. Any coupon-paying bond has a duration shorter than its maturity.

f: How does the textbook want you to handle Macaulay vs. modified duration?
b: It notes both types exist but says CFP Board is unlikely to distinguish them. The duration formula the Board uses is Macaulay (years). For price change you plug that D into −D × [Δy ÷ (1 + y)] — the (1 + y) divisor does the adjusting.

f: What two ways does the textbook calculate a bond's duration?
b:
Formula: Dur = (1+y)/y, minus [(1+y) + t(c − y)] ÷ [c((1+y)t − 1) + y], with y = YTM per period, c = coupon per period, t = periods.
Cash-flow method: Σ(time × PV of each cash flow) ÷ bond price.
Semiannual: halve the rates, double the periods; answer is in periods (÷ 2 for years).

f: What formula estimates a bond's percentage price change from duration?
b:
ΔP/P = −D × [Δy ÷ (1 + y)]
D = duration; Δy = expected rate change (decimal, e.g. 0.0050); y = current YTM — not the coupon. Multiply the result by the current price for the dollar change.

f: What is the quick rule-of-thumb for duration and price change?
b: % price change ≈ −duration × change in rates. A duration-6 bond loses roughly 6% if rates rise 1 point and gains roughly 6% if they fall 1 point.

f: How does the textbook adapt the duration price-change formula for semiannual compounding?
b: Halve the YTM inside the denominator (8% → 1 + 0.04) and leave D and Δy as they are. The extra compounding produces a slightly bigger estimated change than the annual version.

f: A client needs the money in 8 years. Which bond characteristic should you match to that horizon?
b: Duration, not maturity — pick the bond whose duration is closest to 8 years. Aligning duration with the goal's time horizon is how a portfolio is immunized against rate risk.

f: If you expect rates to fall, how should you adjust portfolio duration — and if you expect them to rise?
b: Rates expected to fall → lengthen duration (bigger price gains). Rates expected to rise → shorten it. A very risk-averse client also calls for a lower target duration.

f: Why does duration alone misjudge price changes when rates move a lot?
b: Duration treats the price–yield link as a straight line, which works for small moves (generally under 1%). The real curve bends, so a 2-point move is not simply twice a 1-point move. Convexity measures the gap; total change = duration effect + convexity effect.

f: With positive convexity, how does the actual price change compare with the duration estimate?
b: Rates fall → actual gain is bigger than duration says. Rates rise → actual loss is smaller. Duration understates gains and overstates losses, which is why positive convexity is desirable, especially when rates are volatile.

f: Which bonds typically show negative convexity, and what does that cost the investor?
b: Callable bonds and mortgage-backed bonds. When rates fall they rise less than duration predicts; when rates rise they fall more.

f: Which bond features produce the most convexity?
b: Low coupon, low YTM and long maturity — the same pattern as duration (inverse to coupon and yield, direct with maturity). The Board exam does not ask you to calculate convexity, only to know its effect.

f: Distinguish the balance sheet from the income statement.
b:
Balance sheet: a snapshot at one point in time of assets, liabilities and stockholders' equity.
Income statement (P&L): income and expenses over a period — shows how profitable operations were.

f: What is book value, and why is it rarely the company's fair market value?
b: Assets minus liabilities = stockholders' equity (the company's net worth); ÷ common shares outstanding = book value per share. It rests on historical cost, and inventory methods such as FIFO vs. LIFO change the asset figures.

f: Distinguish top-down from bottom-up fundamental analysis.
b:
Top-down: economy → industry → company.
Bottom-up (the “stock picker”): company fundamentals first (ratio analysis) → industry → economy, which some bottom-up investors skip entirely.

f: Name the four ratio categories and what each one tells you.
b:
• Liquidity (current, quick): can it pay obligations as they come due?
  • Activity (inventory, receivables turnover): how fast assets move through the firm
  • Profitability (ROA, ROE, margins): how well it earns on capital
  • Leverage (debt-to-equity, debt-to-capital): how much it relies on debt

f: What cautions apply when you use ratio analysis?
b: A single ratio means little; compare over time and against peers and industry averages. Diversified firms are hard to place in one industry, and different accounting practices distort comparisons.

f: What does technical analysis rely on, and what does it assume?
b: Only past price and volume data (chartists). It assumes supply and demand set prices, both rational and irrational behavior drive them, prices move in trends that last, and shifts in supply and demand show up in price action before the full effect arrives.

f: What does a narrowing Barron's confidence index signal?
b: The index compares high-grade to lower-grade bond yields. In confident (bull) markets investors reach for yield in lower-quality bonds — a flight from quality — so the yield gap narrows: a bullish signal. A widening gap (flight to quality) is bearish.

f: According to the EMH, where can technical and fundamental analysis add value?
b: Technical analysis: no help in any form (weak, semistrong or strong). Fundamental analysis: can help only if markets are just weak-form efficient.

f: How can an advisor who picks securities with fundamental analysis and MPT still use technical analysis?
b: For trade timing. Because enough technicians act on charts to move prices, the advisor can buy near support or the bottom of a trend line, sell near resistance, or wait for rising on-balance volume before buying a stock already judged cheap.

f: What's the flaw in valuing a stock with a CAPM required return and a guessed growth rate?
b: CAPM uses only the market return, risk-free rate and beta — nothing about the company itself. Without financial statement analysis, g is just a guess. Fundamental analysis tests both and may show expected return falling short of the required return.

f: How does financial leverage affect ROE, ROA and EPS?
b: Debt shrinks the equity base, so the same earnings produce a higher ROE and higher EPS than equity alone would. A low ROA relative to ROE is a telltale sign of heavy leverage. The cost: fixed interest cuts net income and is hard to carry in a contraction.

f: What formula gives the sustainable dividend growth rate?
b:
g = ROE × RR
RR (retention rate) = 1 − dividend payout ratio.
Raise retention and g rises; pay out more and g falls.

f: When should a company keep its earnings rather than pay a high dividend?
b: When it can reinvest internally at a high ROE — retaining earnings then grows future dividends faster. A high payout makes sense only when the firm cannot earn a high return internally. Caveat: very high growth rarely lasts as a company matures.

f: What is the no-growth (perpetuity) dividend discount model, and where is it used?
b: V = D ÷ r. Used when the dividend never changes — most often a preferred stock with a fixed dividend and no maturity. Because there is no maturity, its value is very sensitive to interest rates.

f: State the constant growth (Gordon) model and its key assumptions.
b:
V = D1 ÷ (r − g), with D1 = D0 × (1 + g).
g must be below r (as g nears r, value heads to infinity); r is known and constant; a higher r lowers value. Best for mature companies.

f: What are the steps of the multistage dividend discount model, and when does it fit?
b:
1. Project each dividend until growth settles.
  2. Value the stock with the Gordon model at the point growth settles, using the first constant-growth dividend.
  3. Add that value to the last high-growth year's dividend and take the NPV at r.
Fits growth-phase companies.

f: How do you value a stock that pays no dividends, such as a closely held company?
b:
Discount free cash flow to equity per share: V = FCFE1 ÷ (r − g) = FCFE0(1 + g) ÷ (r − g).
FCFE = operating cash flow − capital investment − debt repayments (including preferred dividends owed).

f: What is the discounted (capitalized) earnings model, and what are its weaknesses?
b: V = E ÷ RD (earnings ÷ capitalization rate). The rate is the reciprocal of the earnings multiple: 10% ↔ 10× earnings. Weaknesses: GAAP earnings are not cash flow and can be managed, and it ignores the residual value of the company's assets.

f: How is the P/E ratio used to judge value and estimate a price?
b: P/E = market price ÷ EPS. Compare with the industry and market P/E: below them suggests undervalued, above suggests overvalued. Estimated price: V = EPS × benchmark P/E.

f: What is the PEG ratio and how is it read?
b: PEG = P/E ÷ g, with g entered as a whole number (10% → 10). It lets you compare companies growing at different rates; supporters view a PEG below 1.00 as good value.

f: What is the textbook's P/FCF formula, and why is free cash flow preferred to earnings?
b: P/FCF = (1 + g) ÷ (r − g). A ratio below peers may justify buying. Free cash flow is favored because accounting earnings can be managed and vary by industry.

f: What is the P/S ratio, and what is its main shortcoming?
b: P/S = price per share ÷ sales per share; below peers suggests value. It ignores net income — a firm can post big sales and still lose money — so it is a weak complement to P/E.

f: Distinguish intrinsic value methods from relative value methods.
b:
Intrinsic (stand-alone): no-growth, constant growth and multistage DDMs; discounted free cash flow.
Relative (comparison): P/E, PEG, P/FCF, P/S.
Intrinsic value above market price → undervalued; below → overvalued.

f: What are the steps for computing a property's net operating income (NOI)?
b:
Gross rents + other income (laundry, parking) = PGI
− vacancy & collection losses = EGI
− cash operating expenses = NOI
Mortgage interest/debt service and depreciation are never subtracted.

f: How is a property's intrinsic value estimated from NOI, and how is the cap rate chosen?
b:
Value = NOI ÷ cap rate.
The cap rate is approximated from the implied cap rates of recent comparable sales, then adjusted for differences between those properties and the subject property (often by an appraiser). The result is the most a prudent buyer should pay.

f: A client buys a $500,000 rental with $50,000 down and later sells it for $550,000. What return did leverage produce on her equity (ignore costs)?
b: ($550,000 − $500,000) ÷ $50,000 = 100%. A 10% price rise is magnified 10× because only 10% of the price was her own money. Leverage magnifies losses the same way.

f: How is undeveloped land taxed while held and when sold?
b: It produces no income (only expenses), so current taxation matters little; property taxes are generally deductible each year. Appreciation is untaxed until a taxable sale, then taxed as capital gain — or ordinary income if the IRS treats the owner as a real estate dealer.

f: Distinguish a RELP from a publicly traded REIT.
b:
• RELP: run by a general partner; usually illiquid, must generally sell the whole interest; income/losses fall under the passive activity rules.
  • REIT: corporation run by a board; shares trade on exchanges, sell any number; income is portfolio (investment) income and losses are capital losses, not passive.

f: What must a REIT do to avoid entity-level federal income tax?
b: Distribute at least 90% of net annual earnings to shareholders and derive at least 75% of gross income from real estate (2026 edition figures). REIT dividends are generally ordinary income, though the text notes they may qualify for the 0%/15%/20% rates (2026 edition figure).

f: In a CMO, which tranche has the least and which the most interest rate risk, and why?
b:
Tranche A: least — it gets all principal first, so it has the shortest repayment period.
Tranche Z: most — it gets nothing until all others are repaid; its interest accrues like a zero-coupon bond and is taxable as earned.

f: What does each of the four basic option positions give or obligate the investor to do?
b:
• Buy call: right to buy at the strike
  • Write call: obligation to sell at the strike if exercised
  • Buy put: right to sell at the strike
  • Write put: obligation to buy at the strike if exercised
One contract = 100 shares; buyers pay the premium, writers receive it.

f: Which two option positions are bullish and which two are bearish?
b:
Bullish: buy a call or write a put.
Bearish: buy a put or write a call.
Memory hook: “call up, put down” for buyers; writers take the opposite view.

f: State the maximum gain and maximum loss for each basic option position.
b:
• Long call: gain unlimited; loss = premium
  • Short call (naked): gain = premium; loss unlimited
  • Long put: gain = strike − premium; loss = premium
  • Short put: gain = premium; loss = strike − premium

f: What are the formulas for intrinsic value of a call and of a put, and for time value?
b:
Call intrinsic = greater of 0 or (stock price − strike)
Put intrinsic = greater of 0 or (strike − stock price)
Time value = premium − intrinsic value
Intrinsic value is never negative.

f: When is an option in, at, or out of the money?
b:
In: intrinsic value > 0 (call: stock above strike; put: stock below strike).
At: stock price = strike.
Out: intrinsic value is zero and stock ≠ strike (call: stock below strike; put: stock above strike).

f: Distinguish the binomial model's price assumption from Black-Scholes'.
b:
Binomial (two-state): the stock moves in discrete up-or-down steps; as steps multiply it approaches Black-Scholes.
Black-Scholes: price changes continuously (geometric Brownian motion), captured by a volatility factor (σ). Both value European calls.

f: Name the five Black-Scholes inputs and which one moves opposite to a call's value.
b:
Stock price ↑, time to expiration ↑, risk-free rate ↑, volatility ↑ → call value ↑.
Exercise price is the inverse one: a higher strike lowers the call's value because the stock must rise further to reach intrinsic value.

f: How is the premium treated for tax when an option is exercised, for the holder and the writer?
b:
Call exercised: holder adds premium to stock basis; writer adds premium to amount realized on the sale.
Put exercised: holder subtracts premium from amount realized; writer subtracts premium from basis of the stock bought.

f: What happens for tax when an option expires unexercised?
b:
Holder: the premium is a capital loss on the expiration date.
Writer: the premium is a short-term capital gain on that date. If the holder instead sells the option, the difference is a capital gain or loss and the writer is unaffected.

f: Why do speculators buy options instead of buying stock on margin, and what is the catch?
b: Leverage: margin purchases need at least 50% cash under Federal Reserve rules (2026 edition figure), while an option may cost as little as ~5% of the stock's value. Max loss is the premium. The catch is a limited life: the stock must move far enough before expiration to overcome the premium.

f: What is the breakeven at expiration for a long call and for a long put?
b:
Long call: strike + premium.
Long put: strike − premium.
Example: $40 call bought for $1.50 needs the stock above $41.50 to profit.

f: What does a covered call writer gain and give up, and when does the strategy work best?
b: Gains the premium (extra income and a small downside cushion); gives up appreciation above the strike, and the shares may be called away. Works best in a sideways market. Premium cushion is minor if the stock falls sharply.

f: How does a protective put work, and what is its main drawback?
b: Own the stock and buy a put: losses below the strike are offset, while upside is kept. Drawback: the premium is a cost that lowers return, and protection lasts only until expiration, so repeated hedging gets expensive. Index puts hedge a whole portfolio.

f: What three positions make up a zero-cost collar, and why is it called zero-cost?
b: Long the stock + buy a put (downside protection) + write a call (premium income). The call premium received pays for the put premium, so the net outlay is roughly zero. Used to protect a gain in a long stock position.

f: Why is naked call writing riskier than naked put writing?
b: A stock's price has no ceiling, so a naked call's loss is theoretically unlimited. A naked put's worst case is the stock going to zero: loss = strike − premium. Writers often sell naked puts on stocks they'd like to own anyway.

f: Distinguish a long straddle, a short straddle, and a spread.
b:
Long straddle: buy a call and a put, same strike and expiration — profits if the stock moves (either way) by more than both premiums.
Short straddle: write both — bets on little movement.
Spread: two or more options with different strikes and/or expirations, betting on a change in their price differential.

f: A client sold a stock short. Which option protects against a price spike, and how?
b: Buy a call. If the stock surges, the call's gain offsets the short-sale loss (capping the otherwise unlimited risk). If the stock drops as hoped, the call expires and its cost reduces the short profit.

f: How does a futures contract differ from buying an option in terms of obligation and loss potential?
b: A futures contract obligates both sides to make or take delivery at a set future price; it is standardized and exchange-traded. Because of high leverage, losses can far exceed the initial deposit. An option buyer can lose only the premium.

f: Distinguish initial margin from maintenance margin in a futures account.
b:
Initial margin (good faith deposit / performance bond): typically about 5–10% of contract value.
Maintenance margin: if equity drops below it, the investor must immediately deposit enough to restore the account to the initial margin level.

f: Distinguish a short hedge from a long hedge.
b:
Short hedge: you own (are long) the asset, so you sell futures to guard against falling prices (farmer, rancher, stock portfolio owner).
Long hedge: you will need to buy (are short) the asset, so you buy futures to guard against rising prices (baker, cereal maker).

f: A bond investor expects interest rates to rise. Should she buy or sell Treasury futures?
b: Sell them. Rising rates push bond prices down, so a short bond futures position gains as her bond portfolio loses. (Expecting falling rates → buy bond futures.)

f: How are gains and losses on futures contracts taxed?
b: Contracts are marked to market at year end; net gain or loss is treated as 60% long-term and 40% short-term capital gain/loss regardless of actual holding period (2026 edition figure). Futures results are capital in character even if the underlying asset would not be.

f: What long-term capital gain rate applies to collectibles, and how does that compare to securities?
b: 28% maximum long-term rate for collectibles (tangibles other than real estate) (2026 edition figure) — higher than the rate on long-term gains from securities.

f: In what ways do tangible assets act as a tax shelter?
b: Gains are untaxed until sale; most produce no income, so no ordinary income tax while held; and if held until death the basis steps up to fair market value, so the built-in gain escapes capital gains tax.

f: Why is gold considered a hedge for stocks, and what environment hurts gold most?
b: Gold's value comes from factors outside financial markets (e.g., inflation fear), so it often moves inversely to stocks. High real interest rates hurt it most (no income, high opportunity cost); negative real rates favor it.

f: What are the three ways to invest in natural resources, and their key tax advantage?
b:
1) Properties/lands, typically via limited partnerships
2) Stocks of resource developers
3) Natural resource sector mutual funds
Advantage: pass-through deductions such as depletion and intangible drilling costs. Risk is high, especially exploratory drilling.

f: What two extra risks does a U.S. investor take on with foreign securities, and what is country risk?
b: Exchange rate (currency) risk and country risk. Country risk is the composite risk of investing in a particular nation — political events (coups, revolutions) and structural policies such as confiscating profits or dividends.

f: List typical traits of emerging markets versus developed markets.
b:
Emerging: low income (GDP) and low equity capitalization, questionable liquidity, currency-conversion and ownership limits, high volatility, unstable institutions, high taxes/commissions, weak transparency — but strong growth prospects. Smaller ones are frontier markets.
Developed: large caps, liquid markets, few currency limits, stable institutions, clear regulation.

f: Distinguish a global fund from an international fund.
b:
Global: U.S. and foreign securities — can overlap holdings a client already owns in domestic funds.
International: non-U.S. securities only — the cleaner choice to diversify away from U.S. companies.

f: A client says his ADRs carry no currency risk because they trade and pay in dollars. What is wrong with that?
b: An ADR is a U.S. bank's trust receipt for foreign shares held by its foreign branch. Its dividends are declared in the local currency and converted, and its price tracks the home-market share, so currency risk remains.

f: During the holding period, should a U.S. investor in a foreign stock want the dollar to rise or fall?
b: Fall against the foreign currency. When the investment is sold, the foreign currency then converts into more dollars. (Before buying, a stronger dollar is welcome because it buys more foreign currency.) A foreign investor in U.S. stocks wants their own currency to fall against the dollar.

f: How do you compute a U.S. investor's holding period return on a foreign security?
b:
1) Dollar cost = foreign price paid ÷ (foreign units per $1) at purchase
2) Dollar proceeds = foreign value at sale ÷ (foreign units per $1) at sale
3) HPR = (proceeds − cost) ÷ cost

f: A quote says $1.25 buys one British pound. How many pounds does $1 buy, and what happens if the dollar devalues?
b: 1 ÷ 1.25 = 0.80 pounds per dollar. A dollar devaluation means $1 buys fewer pounds (and it takes more dollars to buy one pound).

f: According to the textbook, what two things let a diversified investor capture more return per unit of risk?
b:
• Combining assets that have low correlation with one another
  • A longer time horizon
Either one, or both together.

f: Distinguish diversification from asset allocation.
b:
Asset allocation spreads money across asset classes (cash, fixed income, equities, real assets).
Diversification means holding enough different, loosely correlated securities to wash out unsystematic risk — it can happen inside a single class.
Allocating across classes does not by itself guarantee diversification (you could hold one name per class).

f: How many holdings does the textbook treat as enough for a diversified portfolio on the exam?
b:
• 10–15 large-cap stocks in different industries (exam rule)
  • 25–30 mid- or small-cap stocks
  • 4–7 mutual funds in different asset classes
Other studies range up to 100; Figure 6.1 shows the risk curve flattening around 15–20 holdings.

f: Match each risk to the allocation fix the textbook suggests: market, interest rate, business, liquidity.
b:
• Market → spread across all four asset classes (and diversify within equities)
  • Interest rate → stagger bond maturities
  • Business → allocate among classes and use mutual funds
  • Liquidity → keep enough in cash and cash equivalents

f: Why might an investor rationally choose an investment expected to earn 8% over one expected to earn 10%?
b: Return means little without the risk taken to get it. If the 10% option carries far more risk, the 8% option may deliver more return per unit of risk. Taking more risk raises the required return; it does not guarantee a higher realized return.

f: What two components make up total risk, and what statistic measures each?
b:
Total risk = unsystematic (diversifiable) + systematic (nondiversifiable).
Total risk → standard deviation
Systematic risk → beta
Because diversification handles unsystematic risk, systematic risk is the investor's main concern.

f: Name the five systematic risks in the PRIME mnemonic.
b:
• Purchasing power risk
  • Reinvestment rate risk
  • Interest rate risk
  • Market risk
  • Exchange rate risk
All are nondiversifiable.

f: Which unsystematic (diversifiable) risks does the textbook list?
b:
• Business
  • Financial
  • Default (credit)
  • Political
  • Tax
  • Investment manager
  • Liquidity
  • Marketability
They hit a particular company, country or sector and are not correlated with overall market returns. The list is not exhaustive.

f: Distinguish business risk from financial risk.
b:
Business risk — uncertainty in operating income from the way a firm (and its sector) does business.
Financial risk — the chance that the firm's capital structure (debt vs. equity) hurts the value of the equity.
Tell: operations = business; leverage = financial.

f: Is a common stockholder exposed to default risk? Why or why not?
b: No. Default risk is a debt issuer failing to pay interest or principal on time. A corporation has no contractual duty to pay common dividends, so common stock carries no default risk. Junk bonds carry the most default risk.

f: Distinguish liquidity risk from marketability risk.
b:
Liquidity risk — you can't sell quickly without a significant loss of principal (e.g., real estate, closely held business).
Marketability risk — you can't find a ready buyer at all. Active, efficient markets lower both.

f: What actually drives purchasing power risk, and which holdings suffer most?
b:
Unexpected changes in inflation — the current level is already priced in through an inflation premium.
Hits fixed-income holdings, CDs, and cash equivalents hardest because they have little room for principal growth.

f: Which investments carry the most reinvestment rate risk, and what eliminates it?
b:
Most exposed: long-term fixed income when rates are changing, and mortgage-backed securities such as GNMAs (cash flows return early to be reinvested).
Eliminate it with zero-coupon bonds — no interim cash flows to reinvest.

f: For a U.S. investor holding foreign securities, does a weakening dollar help or hurt, and what reduces exchange rate risk?
b:
Helps. Foreign-currency payments convert into more dollars when the dollar weakens; a strengthening dollar shrinks them.
The textbook names Yankee bonds as one way to reduce exchange rate risk.

f: What are the two formulas for beta?
b:
βi = COVim ÷ σm2 = (ρim × σi) ÷ σm
COVim = covariance of asset with market; σm2 = market variance; ρim = correlation with market; σi, σm = standard deviations.

f: How do you read betas of 0.80, 1.0 and 1.30?
b:
• 0.80 — 20% less volatile than the market; defensive
  • 1.0 — the market itself
  • 1.30 — 30% more volatile than the market; aggressive
Beta 0 = no correlation with the market (e.g., short-term T-bills); negative = tends to move opposite (e.g., gold, inverse ETFs).

f: Why does beta become less reliable as an asset's correlation with the market falls?
b: Beta = (σ<sub>i</sub> ÷ σ<sub>m</sub>) × ρ. A low correlation shrinks beta even when the asset is very volatile, so a gold fund can show a low beta without low volatility. Beta fits diversified portfolios; standard deviation fits any asset.

f: How is a portfolio's weighted beta calculated, and what does a result of 1.0 mean?
b:
Weighted beta = Σ (market value weight × beta) for each holding.
1.0 = the portfolio moves in lockstep with the market (like an index fund). Most portfolios land above or below 1.0.

f: How do you compute a portfolio's weighted average return?
b:
Multiply each holding's return by its share of total portfolio value, then add.
Rp = Σ (Wi × Ri), with weights summing to 100%.
Calculator: enter each return with its dollar amount as the weight, then read the weighted mean.

f: What is the formula for the sample standard deviation of historical returns, and how does the population version differ?
b:
Sample: S = √[ Σ(rt − r̄)2 ÷ (n − 1) ]
Population: σ = same, but divide by n.
The exam is likely to ask only for the sample version (calculator Sx, not σx).

f: Under a normal distribution, what share of returns falls within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean?
b:
• ±1 SD → 68%
  • ±2 SD → 95%
  • ±3 SD → 99%
Returns beyond 3 SD are outliers. Half of outcomes fall on each side of the mean.

f: What does a z-statistic measure, and how is it computed?
b:
How many standard deviations a value sits from the mean.
z = (value − mean) ÷ standard deviation
Positive = above the mean; negative = below.

f: When should an investor assume a normal distribution, and when a lognormal one?
b:
Normal — for the range of annual returns, which can be negative or positive.
Lognormal — for the ending (terminal) value of an unleveraged portfolio, which can fall to zero but not below, yet has no upper limit; the mean exceeds the median.

f: Distinguish a positively skewed from a negatively skewed return distribution.
b:
Positive (right-tailed) — long tail on the right; median below mean; more outliers above the mean. Typical of investment returns, and many investors like it.
Negative (left-tailed) — long tail on the left; median above mean; exposes the investor to large losses.

f: Distinguish a leptokurtic from a platykurtic distribution.
b:
Leptokurtic — more peaked than normal; returns cluster near the mean. Preferred by investors who want to minimize volatility.
Platykurtic — flatter than normal; more returns land far from the mean.
Kurtosis = degree of peakedness; skewness = asymmetry.

f: What does semivariance measure, and why do some critics prefer it to standard deviation?
b: The average squared deviation below the mean only. Standard deviation penalizes upside surprises too, while a risk-averse investor mainly cares about downside. Lower semivariance = less likely to suffer a large loss.

f: What is the coefficient of variation formula, and how is it used to choose between investments?
b:
CV = σ ÷ mean return
It measures total risk per unit of return. Lower CV is better. Use it to compare investments whose returns and standard deviations both differ; ignore extra data such as beta.

f: Distinguish the coefficient of variation (CV) from covariance (COV).
b:
CV — risk per unit of return for one asset (σ ÷ mean); a cross-check on an investment choice.
COV — how two assets' returns move together (ρ × σi × σj); the basis for portfolio diversification.

f: What is the covariance formula, and what is its main limitation?
b:
COVij = ρij × σi × σj
It shows whether two assets move together (+) or opposite (−), but it has no boundaries, so its size is hard to interpret. Same sign as the correlation coefficient.

f: How do you get the correlation coefficient from covariance, and what is its range?
b:
R (or ρ) = COVij ÷ (σi × σj)
Range −1.0 to +1.0. It standardizes covariance and measures the strength of the linear relationship. The farther below +1, the more diversification.

f: What is the formula for the standard deviation of a two-asset portfolio?
b:
σp = √[ Wi2σi2 + Wj2σj2 + 2WiWjCOVij ]
W = weights (sum to 100%); COVij = ρijσiσj. Covariance is the most important input.

f: When can you simply weight-average two assets' standard deviations to get the portfolio standard deviation?
b: Only when the correlation is +1.0. At any correlation below +1, portfolio SD is less than the weighted average SD, so the full formula is required. At −1 with equal SDs and a 50/50 split, risk can reach zero.

f: A client owns no funds and finds two with correlations of +0.25 and +0.40 to the S&P 500. Can you conclude they diversify each other?
b: No. Each tells you only how that fund relates to the index. You must compute the two funds' correlation with each other. Correlations also shift over time and tend to rise in falling markets, when diversification is needed most.

f: What does R<sup>2</sup> measure, and how do you find it?
b:
R2 = (correlation coefficient)2.
It is the share of an asset's movement explained by the benchmark — i.e., systematic risk. 1 − R2 = the share from other factors (unsystematic risk).

f: What R<sup>2</sup> threshold makes beta a reliable risk measure for exam purposes?
b: R2 ≥ 0.70 (Morningstar's threshold; correlation of roughly ±0.84). Reliability fades gradually as R2 drops — there is no cliff at 69. Below it, measure beta against a better-fitting benchmark or use standard deviation.

f: Which portfolio performance measures need an R<sup>2</sup> of about 0.70 or more, and which works at any R<sup>2</sup>?
b:
Treynor and Jensen use beta, so they assume a diversified portfolio and need R2 ≈ 0.70+.
Sharpe uses standard deviation, so it works at any R2 and is required below 0.70.

f: Distinguish a simple rate of return from a compound rate of return.
b:
Simple: total return for the holding period ÷ years held → an annualized, noncompounded rate that ignores the time value of money (45% over 6 years = 7.5%/yr).
Compound: assumes all interim proceeds (interest, principal repaid) are reinvested; solve with the TVM or cash-flow/IRR keys.

f: What are the formulas for the arithmetic mean and the geometric mean of a series of periodic returns?
b:
AM = (r1 + r2 + … + rn) ÷ n — no compounding.
GM = [(1 + r1)(1 + r2)…(1 + rn)]1/n − 1 — assumes compounding.
Calculator: PV = −1, FV = product of the (1 + r) terms, N = n, solve I/YR.

f: Which is larger, the arithmetic or geometric mean, and which should you use to describe a security's track record?
b: The geometric mean is always lower, except when every period's return is identical (then they are equal), because the arithmetic mean ignores compounding. The geometric mean is the preferred measure of a security's historical return.

f: Distinguish a time-weighted return from a dollar-weighted return.
b:
Time-weighted: ignores the investor's later deposits and withdrawals → measures the investment (the manager). Most reported mutual fund returns are time-weighted because managers cannot control shareholder flows.
Dollar-weighted: an IRR that includes every contribution and withdrawal → measures the investor's result; usually differs from the TWR.

f: How do you lay out the cash flows for a dollar-weighted (IRR) return when the investor buys more shares along the way?
b: CF0 = −initial purchase. Each later CF = income received − new purchases (+ any sales). Final CF = value of all shares then held. Solve IRR. For quarterly or monthly flows, the textbook annualizes by multiplying the periodic IRR by periods per year (e.g., × 4).

f: What formula does the CFP exam expect for the real (inflation-adjusted) rate of return?
b:
Real = [(1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1] × 100.
Nominal minus inflation is only an approximation; over long projections such as a retirement needs analysis the shortcut can produce a large dollar error.

f: How do you compute an after-tax, inflation-adjusted rate of return?
b:
1. After-tax = nominal × (1 − marginal tax rate) — include state tax if the state taxes the income.
2. Real after-tax = [(1 + after-tax rate) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1] × 100.
Ex: 7% bond, 30% combined rate, 2.5% inflation → 4.9% → 2.34%.

f: Distinguish the APR from the effective annual rate (EAR), and give the EAR formula.
b:
APR = periodic rate × periods per year; ignores compounding (1.5%/month = 18% APR).
EAR = (1 + i ÷ n)n − 1, where i = stated annual rate and n = compounding periods per year. EAR exceeds the APR whenever compounding occurs more than once a year (18% monthly → 19.56%).

f: What is the HPR formula, and why can't an HPR by itself be compared across investments?
b:
HPR = (ending value − beginning value ± cash flows) ÷ beginning value. Alternate: [(1 + r1)(1 + r2)…(1 + rn)] − 1.
It ignores timing and length of ownership: held more than a year, it overstates the annual return; held less than a year, it understates it.

f: What does total return include, and which kind of client usually prefers each component?
b: Income (dividends or interest) + capital appreciation over the period, usually one year. A recent retiree who needs cash flow tends to value income; a young earner in a high bracket tends to prefer capital growth. Tax status and cash-flow needs drive the preference.

f: What is a mutual fund's SEC yield, and why is it useful?
b: A standardized yield the SEC requires funds to report and disclose in the prospectus: the interest and dividends earned over the most recent 30-day period (2026 edition figure), after expenses. Because every fund computes it the same way, it allows apples-to-apples yield comparisons.

f: What is the formula for Jensen's alpha, and what does its sign tell you?
b:
αp = rp − [rf + (rm − rf)βp] — actual return minus the CAPM required return.
Positive = manager added value for the risk taken (plots above the SML); negative = underperformed (below the SML). It is an absolute measure; beta-based, so for diversified portfolios.

f: What is the Treynor ratio formula, and when is it appropriate?
b: Tp = (rp − rf) ÷ βp. Uses beta, so only for diversified portfolios (or stocks held within them) and only when beta is reliable (R² ≥ 0.70). It is relative: higher is better, and it means something only when compared with another portfolio or the benchmark.

f: What is the Sharpe ratio formula, and why can it be used in almost any situation?
b: S<sub>p</sub> = (r<sub>p</sub> − r<sub>f</sub>) ÷ σ<sub>p</sub>. Its denominator is standard deviation (total risk), so it does not depend on a reliable beta — it works for diversified or undiversified portfolios and single securities. Relative measure: higher = better risk-adjusted return.

f: A fund's R² with the market is 0.55. Which risk-adjusted measure should you rely on, and why?
b: The Sharpe ratio. With R² below 0.70, beta is not reliable, so anything built on beta — the Treynor ratio and Jensen's alpha — is suspect and needs further investigation.

f: Why can an undiversified portfolio look strong under Treynor or Jensen yet weak under Sharpe?
b: Treynor and Jensen measure risk with beta (market risk only), so the large unsystematic risk of an undiversified portfolio is invisible to them. Sharpe uses standard deviation, which captures that extra risk and pulls the ratio down.

f: What's wrong with selecting funds by ranking Sharpe ratios across every asset class?
b: High Sharpe ratios cluster in asset classes that did well recently and do not predict future results. A cross-class ranking would screen out a lagging class (e.g., emerging markets) entirely, wrecking diversification. Compare Sharpe ratios only among funds in the same asset class.

f: What is the information ratio formula, and how is it interpreted?
b: IR = (R<sub>P</sub> − R<sub>B</sub>) ÷ σ<sub>A</sub> — active return over active risk, where σ<sub>A</sub> = standard deviation of the excess return (tracking error). Higher = manager better exploited opportunities; 0.50 or more is often top-quartile. Becomes the Sharpe ratio if the benchmark is a risk-free asset; use only when alpha is positive and beta is meaningful.

f: Distinguish a price-weighted index from a market-capitalization-weighted index.
b:
Price-weighted (DJIA): higher-priced shares move the index more — a $60 stock counts three times a $20 stock.
Cap-weighted (S&P 500, Russell 2000, most indices): weight = firm's market value ÷ index market value ($30B in a $300B index = 10% of the movement); adjusts automatically for splits and stock dividends.
